newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Labour pledges rail regulatory clampdown.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Labour pledges rail regulatory clampdown.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party has pledged a regulatory clampdown on the rail industry, citing the rail franchise operators and Railtrack Plc as the most likely targets for a tougher approach.

Labour's transport spokesman Andrew Smith said in an interview with Reuters that he would activate maximum existing regulatory powers and consider possible new powers to force Railtrack, in particular, to fulfil its investment commitments.

"The first thing to do is use the regulator's powers to the full to enforce Railtrack's investment and management obligations. We're prepared to strengthen its powers to ensure Railtrack invests what it promised and make it deliver," said Smith.
He said the full powers were not currently being utilised against Railtrack to force it to meet its investment obligations.
But he said there were two options which were possible without seeking new legislation.

"At the moment the maximum powers available are not used - they are intricate and complicated. But the regulator can initiate a change to Railtrack's license and can also seek to amend its track access conditions."
The change to the licence refers to its price review which is next due in 2001. This could be tightened if Railtrack refuses to comply with its obligations.

On the track access conditions, which govern payments made by the 25 passenger rail franchises to Railtrack for use of its infrastructure, Smith said another more immediate course of action was to give the franchises more influence.

"The track access conditions could be amended to reflect fulfilment of commitment to invest. This would give a path of recourse for Railtrack's non-compliance to the TOCs (train operating companies or franchises)."

A third option which could be used and which would require primary legislation is understood to be a new legal obligation to make investments. This could even allow for a target or minimum investment requirement, industry figures suggest.
Smith said it was crucial Railtrack lived up to its pledges. "There is already a 700 million stg backlog. Railtrack is a national monopoly and its investment is critical nationwide.
"We certainly won't be deflected by any delaying tactics which may be used by Railtrack."

On the franchises themselves, Smith said the huge number of cancellations made in recent weeks by South West Trains, owned by Stagecoach Holdings Plc SGC L, was another example of regulatory weakness.
"There has to be tough, effective pro-active enforcement of franchise conditions. This involves having a good early warning system and vigorous action.
"The penalty regime is not being used to the full - one of the proofs is the South West Trains affair.
He also reiterated that there was logic to bringing the regulatory functions of the franchising operations together with the rail regulator.
